sections.html:
Most Schenectady houses were built for mill and plant workers, so a listing here turns on age, permits and tenant history more than on new finishes. The city is the seat of Schenectady County, on the Mohawk River about 15 miles northwest of Albany. Its 10.79 square miles hold 6,212.7 people per square mile, so lots are narrow and neighbors are close. You see rows of frame two-families near the old plant sites and larger homes near Union College.

Winters are cold, with January averaging near 22.9 °F, so a house that has been through many heating seasons shows it in roofs, porches and boilers. Buyers look at those first.

Prices are low and renters outnumber owners. Only 45.6% of homes are lived in by their owners, a typical owner-occupied unit is valued at $168,800, and monthly rent is $1,145. A cash investor or small landlord is a natural buyer for many of these houses.

A citywide figure will not price your own address. A house that needs a roof or a new furnace sells for less than its block average, and one with fresh systems sells for more. Ask the assessor for your assessed value and compare it with recent sales on your street.

Value follows history here. The Stockade Historic District, designated in 1965 as New York's first historic district, preserves dozens of Dutch and English colonial houses. The General Electric Realty Plot beside Union College was drawn up for company executives and is counted among the nation's earliest planned residential neighborhoods.

The riverfront looks different from a decade ago. Rivers Casino and Resort opened in February 2017 on a former locomotive works site, and the same development brought a marina, hotels, apartments and condominiums.

If you are selling inside a historic district, speak to the building department before repainting for showings. Painting is among the few jobs the city exempts from permits, and the exemption stops at historic district lines.

sections.h2: Permits for repairs before you list
sections.html:
Nearly every repair, alteration or addition needs a building permit from the City of Schenectady Building Department, and painting is the notable exception. Permits run for 12 months. When you hire a contractor, the department's rule is that the contractor files for the permit, not you. It accepts applications online, by mail to Room 17 at 105 Jay Street, or by fax, and asks you to allow at least 24 hours for processing.

Skipping a permit risks a stop work order and fines, and it can stall a closing if the buyer's lender wants a certificate of completion or occupancy. A Certificate of Ordinary Repair lists small jobs a homeowner can do without a permit. Questions about a specific repair go to 518-382-5050.

  • Expect to supply a scope of work, materials, dimensions and a cost estimate.
  • Electrical and plumbing jobs call for contractors with the required trade credentials where they apply.
  • Workers compensation coverage, or a personal waiver for self-performed work, is part of the packet.
  • Pools need both a building permit and an electrical permit, obtained by the installer.

sections.h2: Selling a house with tenants or a rental history
sections.html:
The city treats any house rented to tenants as a registered rental, and each tenancy needs its own certificate. Landlord registration is step one. The form calls for verified owner information, a named agent if the owner lives outside Schenectady County, a current insurance declaration or bond, and a notary's signature.

Step two is the rental inspection, at $50 per unit. Multi-unit buildings are inspected unit by unit, while single-family rental homes and owner-occupied two-families are exempt from the inspection. Passing earns a rental certificate valid for the present tenancy, or up to three years in a building with three or more units. A new certificate is required whenever one tenant leaves and another arrives, and if no tenant is recorded within 30 days of an inspection, the unit must be inspected again.

Buyers of two- and three-family houses tend to ask for this paper trail, so pull your registration and certificates before you list. Renting without a current certificate violates the city code and can bring fines, fees and possibly jail. A cash buyer will still ask what the file looks like, but can usually take the property as is.

sections.h2: Tax bills, installments and assessment appeals
sections.html:
The city bills once a year, on January 1, and accepts payment in four installments due in January, April, July and October. That single bill rolls together city and county tax, water and sewer charges, and the trash fee where one applies. School tax is billed separately by the school district.

The City Assessment Office in Room 8 at City Hall handles disputes; its number is 518-382-5075. Each year the grievance window opens on May 1, when the tentative roll comes out, and closes late in May. Applications can be mailed, emailed or handed in, and an owner who skips the board hearing is not penalized for it.

Closing figures split the installments between buyer and seller by date. Call the Bureau of Receipts in Room 100 ahead of time and ask for the paid-through status of each quarter.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and filing the deed
sections.html:
New York charges two dollars per five hundred of price on a conveyance, and the seller normally bears it. Buyers pay an extra 1% only on residences at $1 million or above. The return, Form TP-584, goes to the Schenectady County Clerk, and the form and money are due by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered.

One wrinkle for investors: when an LLC buys or sells a building of up to four units, the state will not take the return without documents naming the LLC's members, managers and other authorized people.

sections.h2: A quick checklist before you list
sections.html:
Walk through the house and make a short list of anything a buyer or inspector will notice: roof, porch, boiler, wiring. Then call the Building Department at 518-382-5050 to learn what permits are open at your address. Gather the rental registration and certificates if tenants have lived there, and ask the Bureau of Receipts for the paid-through status of your tax installments.

With that folder ready, you can decide between a listing and a direct cash offer. A listing suits a house in good shape on a block with strong recent sales. A cash offer suits a house that needs work, has tenants you would rather not manage through showings, or has an open permit you do not want to finish.

faqs.q: Will open code violations stop a Schenectady sale?
faqs.a: They will not stop one by law, but they travel with the house. Ask the Building Department what is open at your address and hand buyers a written list before they sign.

faqs.q: Who covers the state transfer tax?
faqs.a: The seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise, at two dollars per five hundred of price. If the seller does not pay, the state looks to the buyer, who can then recover it from the seller.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental certificate to close on a rented house?
faqs.a: Closing does not require one, yet renting without a current certificate breaks city code. Lenders and buyers of multi-unit houses often want to see the registration and certificates.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my assessment?
faqs.a: Each May. The window opens May 1 and closes late in the month. Call the assessment office at 518-382-5075 for the exact date.

faqs.q: Where does the TP-584 transfer form go?
faqs.a: To the Schenectady County Clerk, with payment, by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered. Most closing attorneys and title agents file it together with the deed.
